title: break, continue and pass
intro: `break` leaves a loop straight away. `continue` skips the rest of this pass and moves to the next one. `pass` does nothing — it holds a place where Python needs a statement. A loop can also have an `else` block, which runs only if the loop finished **without** `break`.

questions.prompt: Here the loop stops at the first digit. The `else` would run only if no digit were found.
questions.explanation: `isdigit()` is a string method that's True for `0`–`9`.

questions.prompt: Find the first digit character in `text` and store it in `first_digit`. Use a `for` loop with `break` (`ch.isdigit()` tells you if a character is a digit).

tests.name: value
tests.code:
expected = next((c for c in text if c.isdigit()), None)
assert first_digit == expected, 'first_digit should be the first digit character in text.'

questions.hint: Inside the loop: if it's a digit, store it, then `break`.
questions.explanation: `break` stops at the first match instead of carrying on to the end.

questions.prompt: What does this print? (It's one line.)
questions.explanation: 3 and 6 are skipped; everything else is printed.

questions.prompt: Build `squashed`: the characters of `text` without its spaces. Use a `for` loop with `continue` to skip spaces.
questions.setupCode: text = "c o d e  b r e a k"

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert squashed == text.replace(' ', ''), 'squashed should be text without any spaces.'

questions.hint: If the character is a space, `continue`. Otherwise add it to `squashed`.
questions.explanation: `continue` keeps the main work un-indented and easy to read.

questions.prompt: When does a loop's `else` block run?

options.text: Only if the loop never ran
Only if the loop finished without `break`

questions.explanation: `else` on a loop means *the loop ran to the end without breaking*.

questions.prompt: `found` should be True when `word` contains a `z`, but it only ever checks the first letter. Fix it.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert found == ('z' in word), 'found should be True when word contains z.'
tests.message: found should say whether word contains z.

questions.hint: Where is `break` indented? It should only run once a `z` is found.
questions.explanation: Indentation decides which block a line belongs to — here it decides when the loop stops.

questions.prompt: Python needs a statement in the empty branch. Fill in the keyword that does nothing.
questions.explanation: `pass` keeps the code valid while you decide what goes there.

questions.prompt: Check whether `n` is **prime** (only divisible by 1 and itself). Try every divisor from 2 to `n - 1`; use `break` and the loop's `else` to set `is_prime`.

tests.name: value
tests.code:
expected = n > 1 and all(n % d for d in range(2, n))
assert is_prime == expected, 'is_prime should be True only if no number from 2 to n - 1 divides n.'

questions.hint: On the first divisor found: `is_prime = False`, then `break`. The `else` handles *no divisor found*.
questions.explanation: Loop `else` is made for search loops: it runs only when nothing was found.
The loop broke, so the `else` is skipped.

questions.prompt: Allow up to 3 tries at the password `secret`. Ask with `input("Password? ")`. On the right answer print `Welcome!` and stop asking. If all 3 are wrong, print `Locked out`. Use `for`, `break` and `else`.

tests.name: welcome
tests.code: assert __output__.strip().endswith('Welcome!'), 'Print Welcome! as soon as the right password is typed.'
tests.message: Print Welcome! on the right password.

tests.name: stops
tests.code: assert __output__.count('Password? ') == 2 and 'Locked out' not in __output__, 'Stop asking once the password is right, and don’t print Locked out.'

questions.hint: `break` on success; the loop's `else` prints `Locked out`.
questions.explanation: Loop `else` neatly handles *ran out of tries*.
